prompt.system:
You merge three profiles of the same prize-committee member into one integrated profile. Three different language
models (A, O and G) wrote them independently from their own knowledge, without web access, so each profile can
contain errors, gaps or outdated information.

- Use only what the three profiles say. Do not add facts, works, years, coauthors or roles from your own knowledge.
- For every field, interest and work, list in "support" the letters of the profiles that state it (A, O, G). Merge
  entries that describe the same thing (the same work under slightly different titles, the same field in other
  words); keep the title, year and venue that most profiles agree on.
- Where the profiles disagree on a detail (a year, a venue, a coauthor, a role), keep the better-supported version and
  describe the disagreement in that entry's "conflict" and in "disagreements"; otherwise "conflict" is "".
- Keep entries that only one profile states, with that single letter. Drop an entry only if it clearly belongs to a
  different person (a namesake) or contradicts the member's affiliation, and say so in "caveats".
- Write the integrated persona from what the profiles share; where they diverge, keep the better-supported view and
  name the alternative in "support_note". Keep the persona grounded in the record; do not predict whom the member
  will support for the 2026 prize.
- "caveats": what a reader should check before relying on the profile (single-profile or low-confidence items,
  knowledge cutoffs, possible namesakes, a profile that did not recognize the person).

representative_works.title: Optimal Taxes on Fossil Fuel in General Equilibrium
representative_works.contribution: Derived a simple closed-form optimal carbon tax formula in a dynamic general-equilibrium climate-economy model.

representative_works.title: Long-Run Implications of Investment-Specific Technological Change
representative_works.contribution: Quantified the role of investment-specific technical change, measured through relative equipment prices, in postwar US growth.

representative_works.title: Vested Interests in a Positive Theory of Stagnation and Growth
representative_works.contribution: Political-economy growth model in which vested interests in existing technologies block adoption of new ones.

representative_works.title: On the Size of U.S. Government: Political Economy in the Neoclassical Growth Model
representative_works.contribution: Embeds voting and redistribution in a neoclassical growth model to study the political-economy determinants of government size.

representative_works.title: Equilibrium Welfare and Government Policy with Quasi-Geometric Discounting
representative_works.contribution: Studies welfare and policy when agents have present-biased preferences.

representative_works.title: Consumption-Savings Decisions with Quasi-Geometric Discounting
representative_works.contribution: Analyzed equilibria and indeterminacy in savings problems with time-inconsistent (quasi-hyperbolic) preferences.

representative_works.title: Revisiting the Welfare Effects of Eliminating Business Cycles
representative_works.contribution: Reassesses the welfare cost of business cycles in a model with idiosyncratic risk and labor-market elements, showing that heterogeneity matters.

representative_works.title: Is Piketty's 'Second Law of Capitalism' Fundamental?
representative_works.contribution: Argued from standard growth theory that capital-income ratios need not explode as growth slows.

representative_works.title: Gross Worker Flows over the Business Cycle
representative_works.contribution: Model of flows among employment, unemployment and nonparticipation that matches cyclical labor-market dynamics.

representative_works.title: Labor Supply in the Past, Present, and Future: A Balanced-Growth Perspective
representative_works.contribution: Growth model with preferences that generate a secular decline in hours worked, consistent with historical data.

representative_works.title: Directed Technical Change as a Response to Natural Resource Scarcity
representative_works.contribution: Shows how natural-resource scarcity directs innovation toward resource-saving technologies, linking growth theory, energy and environmental macro.

persona.summary: A leading quantitative macroeconomist who combines rigorous dynamic general-equilibrium theory with disciplined quantitative evaluation. His work spans heterogeneous agents and inequality, technology and growth, fiscal and political economy, time-inconsistent preferences, and climate economics. He is an experienced member of the prize committee and serves as secretary in 2026. The persona is inferred from his research record.
persona.research_lens: Structural and general-equilibrium. He asks how individual heterogeneity, incentives, technology and policy constraints aggregate into macroeconomic outcomes, and whether a mechanism survives general-equilibrium feedback.
persona.methods_and_evidence: Dynamic programming and recursive equilibrium theory, numerical solution methods, and calibration to macro and micro moments. He runs quantitative counterfactual, welfare and policy experiments, and seeks analytical tractability where possible, as in the closed-form carbon tax. He is not primarily identified with reduced-form microeconometrics (O).
persona.what_they_value_in_contributions:
- Durable tools or frameworks that the profession widely adopts, as with the Krusell–Smith method.
- Methodological breakthroughs that make intractable problems solvable.
- Tight links between theory and credible quantitative magnitudes.
- Mechanisms rather than correlations or accounting identities.
- Policy-relevant and welfare implications from internally consistent models.
- Broad influence across subfields such as inequality, public finance, labor and climate.
likely_questions_in_deliberation: Does the result hold in general equilibrium, or is it a partial-equilibrium effect that fades once prices, policy and expectations adjust?
Did the work change the models or computational methods economists actually use, i.e., is it a workhorse?
Are the magnitudes quantitatively important and credible, not just theoretically possible?
Does the contribution handle heterogeneity, risk and distributional consequences credibly, including across agents or regions?
Can the framework support disciplined welfare or policy counterfactuals?
If the contribution is empirical, what is the economic mechanism and can it be integrated into a coherent equilibrium model?
Is the contribution attributable to the nominated individuals, and how does it relate to predecessors?
Does the work speak to long-run issues such as growth, technology, inequality or climate?
